content.text:
I found five em dashes and a handful of other AI tells. Most of the copy is in [page.tsx](app/page.tsx), plus a few lines in `layout.tsx` and `StepArt.tsx`.

## Em dashes (5)
- [layout.tsx:9](app/layout.tsx:9): the page title, "Earshot — live AI captions for any video"
- [page.tsx:67](app/page.tsx:67): "…any video that plays in the page — no YouTube captions required."
- [page.tsx:100](app/page.tsx:100): "…press Share — and only that tab."
- [page.tsx:177](app/page.tsx:177): "Captions appear as words are spoken — usually in under a second."
- [StepArt.tsx:56](components/StepArt.tsx:56): "Earshot asks Chrome to listen to this tab — nothing else."

## Other copy smells
- **A dramatic add-on after the dash.** "— and only that tab" and "— nothing else" have the same shape: a point, then an emphatic reassurance tacked on. Together they say the same thing twice.
- **A cute parallel headline.** "Your audio, your call" ([page.tsx:98](app/page.tsx:98)) is a very common AI section title.
- **Lists of three everywhere:**
  - "search, click to jump back, and download" (line 38)
  - "Any YouTube video, Short or livestream" (line 74)
  - "searchable, clickable transcript" in the meta description
- **"No X required"** (line 68) is a stock tagline phrase.
- **Hype filler words:**
  - "right here in Earshot's player" (line 74)
  - "right on youtube.com" (line 112)
  - "ends it instantly" (line 103)
  - "powered by Deepgram Nova-3" in the meta description
- **An overclaim the page then walks back.** The headline says "for **any** video." Line 112 says some videos can't be played outside YouTube, and the footer says it only works in Chrome and Edge on desktop. The "AI" in the headline is also buzzwordy, since nobody picks captions because they're AI.
- **The product as a person.** "Earshot listens along" and "Earshot hears the video" turn the app into a character. "Transcripts live in your browser tab" does the same.
- **The same line twice.** "Paste a YouTube video or livestream" appears in both the hero (line 38) and the meta description.

## Layout and design smells
- **The default AI landing page structure:** a hero with a big headline, a subhead and an input; then a "How it works" section with three numbered steps and illustration cards; then a two-card grid; then a two-item footer.
- **The default styling:** a dark theme with one warm accent color, `rounded-3xl` cards with a 1px ring, a radial gradient behind the preview, and a pulsing "Live captions" badge. Bricolage Grotesque with Inter is also a font pairing that AI tools reach for constantly.
- **Developer instructions in a card for visitors.** The extension card ([page.tsx:115-128](app/page.tsx:115)) gives `npm run build` steps. That reads like a README pasted into the page, not something a visitor can act on.

## What isn't a problem
- The curly quotes and the "Try one:" example chips are fine.
- The caption preview that writes itself in is a real, specific detail. Keep it.

content.text:
Nothing's edited yet. Here's what I'd change each line to, so you can approve or redline first.

**Page title** ([layout.tsx:9](app/layout.tsx:9))
- Before: Earshot — live AI captions for any video
- After: Earshot: live captions for YouTube

**Meta description**
- Before: Paste a YouTube video or livestream and get real-time captions and a searchable, clickable transcript, powered by Deepgram Nova-3.
- After: Live captions and a transcript for YouTube videos and streams that don't have captions.

**Hero headline**
- Before: Live AI captions for any video.
- After: Captions for videos that don't have them.

**Hero subhead**
- Before: Paste a YouTube video or livestream. Earshot listens along and writes captions as people speak, plus a transcript you can search, click to jump back, and download.
- After: Paste a YouTube link and captions show up as people talk. You also get a transcript. Click any line to jump back to that moment.

**How it works intro** (line 67)
- Before: Earshot hears the video through Chrome's tab sharing, so it works with any video that plays in the page — no YouTube captions required.
- After: It uses Chrome's tab sharing to hear the video's audio. The video doesn't need captions of its own.

**Step 1** (line 74)
- Before: Any YouTube video, Short or livestream. It plays right here in Earshot's player.
- After: Videos, Shorts and livestreams all work. The video plays on this page.

**Step 2** ([StepArt.tsx:56](components/StepArt.tsx:56))
- Before: Earshot asks Chrome to listen to this tab — nothing else.
- After: Chrome will ask which tab to share.

**Privacy card heading** (line 98)
- Before: Your audio, your call
- After: Privacy

**Privacy bullets**
- Before: Earshot only hears a tab after you pick it and press Share — and only that tab.
- After: Earshot can only hear the tab you share.
- Before: Audio streams to Deepgram for transcription while captions are on. Stop captions, or Chrome's "Stop sharing", ends it instantly.
- After: While captions are on, the audio goes to Deepgram to be transcribed. Stopping captions, or clicking "Stop sharing" in Chrome, cuts it off.
- Before: Transcripts live in your browser tab and disappear when you close it. Nothing is stored on a server.
- After: Transcripts aren't saved anywhere. Close the tab and they're gone.

**Caption preview note** (line 177)
- Before: Captions appear as words are spoken — usually in under a second.
- After: Captions usually show up less than a second after someone speaks.

**Extension card** (lines 110–128)
- Before: the "Captions on youtube.com itself" heading, a short pitch, then three `npm run build` steps.
- After: keep the heading and one sentence: "Some videos won't play outside YouTube. The Chrome extension captions them on youtube.com." Then add a "Setup instructions" link to the README instead of the build steps.

**Footer:** no change. It's already plain.

Two choices for you:
1. **The headline.** "Captions for videos that don't have them" says why someone would use Earshot. If you'd rather it say what Earshot is, "Live captions for YouTube" is the safer option.
2. **The layout.** These rewrites change the words only. I could also break up the template structure (hero, three steps, two cards), but that's a bigger change.

content.text:
Yes, I can see it. I opened the shot in the browser pane. The preview is an animated, fairly low-resolution image, so small text is blurry, but the layout is clear. (The em dash fix is already pushed to `main` as `6250625`.)

**What the design looks like**
- **Light theme.** It's off-white with soft greens, the opposite of Earshot's dark theme with amber.
- **A floating card layout.** The whole landing page sits inside a rounded white card. Behind it is a full-bleed 3D scene of a grassy hill, with a blurred green glow around the edges.
- **Hero on the left.** It has a big, bold sans-serif headline. The words "AI video" are in a lime-green accent color with a small "+" in front. Below that are a short paragraph, a pill-shaped lime button with a "Watch the tour" link beside it, and a row of overlapping avatars for social proof.
- **Images on the right.** A few rounded photo cards are scattered at slight angles over the landscape, with small avatar bubbles pinned to them. It reads like people collaborating on a canvas.
- **Minimal navigation.** It's a logo, four small links, "Login" and a black pill "Get a demo" button.

**What could carry over to Earshot**
- The light, airy, single-card look would set Earshot apart from the dark template it uses now.
- The scattered image cards could show caption snippets on video frames instead of the static preview.
- The colored phrase in the headline would work if the wording earns it.

**What to watch out for**
- **AI smells of its own.** The paragraph text in the shot (as far as it's readable) has the same tone you're trying to get rid of. The colored "+AI" headline and the avatar row are also common Dribbble tropes. I'd take the visual direction, not the copy.
- **It's a mockup, not a working page.** The 3D landscape would need a real image or video asset.
- **It's someone else's work.** Kris Anfalova designed it. Using it as inspiration for direction and mood is fine. Copying it pixel for pixel isn't.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rizelscarlett/.claude/skills/frontend-design

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

{/* Privacy + extension */}

Your audio, your call

  • Earshot only hears a tab after you pick it and press Share, and it only hears that tab.
  • Audio streams to Deepgram for transcription while captions are on. Stop captions, or Chrome’s “Stop sharing”, ends it instantly.
  • Transcripts live in your browser tab and disappear when you close it. Nothing is stored on a server.

Captions on youtube.com itself

Some videos can’t be played outside YouTube. The Earshot Chrome extension captions them right on youtube.com, with a side panel transcript.

content.text:
I've applied the Dribbble shot's ideas to the Earshot home page, and it's running in the browser pane. I checked it at desktop width and on a phone-sized screen, with no console errors. The page typechecks and the watch page still loads. Nothing is committed.

**What I took from the shot**
- **Light theme.** The home page now uses off-white and soft greens instead of near-black and amber.
- **A white card on a landscape.** The hero sits in a rounded white card. Behind it is a pale sky over layered green hills, drawn in code, and the hills show along the right side.
- **Tilted media cards across the card's edge.** In Earshot's version they're captioned videos instead of stock photos:
  - The TED stage, with its caption writing in word by word as before.
  - A small livestream card with a red "Live" badge and the caption "[soft piano music]". Captions describe sound too, not just speech.
  - A transcript card searched for "creativity", with the match highlighted.
- **Pill buttons** and a dark "Chrome extension" button in the top right.

**Where I went my own way**
- **No colored "+AI" word in the headline.** That's one of the tells you're trying to get rid of.
- **No avatar row**, since Earshot has no users to show off.
- **A different font.** The home page now uses Atkinson Hyperlegible Next. It was designed to be easy to read for people with low vision, which suits a captioning tool.

**How it's built**
- The light theme is scoped with a `.theme-field` class in [globals.css](src/app/globals.css). It flips the shared color variables to light, so the URL box, logo and step illustrations restyle themselves.
- The watch page and the Chrome extension keep the dark theme. Video players read better on dark backgrounds.
- The new hero is in [page.tsx](src/app/page.tsx), in `Hills` and `HeroScatter`.

**Not changed yet**
- The copy, apart from the em dashes you already removed.
- The structure below the hero ("How it works" and the two cards). It just picks up the light colors.
- The browser theme color in `layout.tsx` is still dark, so the browser bar on phones will look dark against the light page.

content.text:
You're right, that first pass was lazy. I only looked at a still image of the shot, copied its light look, and didn't check spacing or framing carefully. I threw all of it out and started again from the dark version you had. This time I played the shot's 7-second video frame by frame and worked from its animation and layout, not its colors or words.

The new version is open in the browser pane. Nothing is committed.

**What I took from the shot**
- **Layout: one scene with the text panel floating inside it.** On desktop the hero is a single dark video stage. The headline, link box and example links sit on a solid black panel inside its left half. The right half is the "video": a speaker under a spotlight.
- **Animation: the scene builds itself in order,** like things being placed on a canvas one at a time:
  1. The stage starts blurred and comes into focus.
  2. The text panel slides in.
  3. The player controls appear: Stop captions, captions on/off, transcript, full screen. These match the real buttons on the watch page.
  4. The caption writes itself in word by word, and its black background grows with each word like a real caption.
  5. A transcript card appears in the top corner, and its lines arrive one by one, with the current line highlighted in amber.

  With reduced motion turned on, everything shows without animating.

**The problems you pointed out**
- **Double borders.** The stage is the only frame. The panel inside it has no border of its own, just a solid fill. On phones there's no outer frame at all: the text sits directly on the page, and the stage is a single frame below it.
- **Too big.** The headline is now 52px on desktop instead of 68–72px, and the body text is smaller.
- **Spacing and centering.** The hero uses the same centered width and side margins as the rest of the page. The panel's content is centered vertically, and the gap before "How it works" is smaller. At 375px wide nothing runs off the side.

**Not changed**

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

content.text:
I've rebuilt the hero on your reference's layout in dark mode. It's open in the browser pane. Nothing is committed.

**Left side (the panel)**
- A solid black panel inside a dimly lit stage. The Earshot logo sits top left, with "How it works" and "Privacy" beside it.
- Below that, the headline, the subhead, and the "Paste a YouTube link" box with the "Watch with captions" button.
- "Or try one" sits at the bottom of the panel, where your reference has its team row. Each example has a round icon, like the avatars in the reference: a play button for the TED talk and a pulsing red dot for the livestream.
- A light "Get the Chrome extension" button sits top right, where the reference has "Get a demo".

**Right side (real pieces of Earshot)**
- **Video frame:** the captions write in word by word, with a "Live captions" badge and a progress bar. A round amber sound meter is pinned to its corner, like the avatar circles in the reference.
- **Chrome extension popup:** copied from the real popup, showing the Live badge, "AI captions" switched on, and "Captioning this tab on youtube.com". It's tilted slightly, like the overlapping photo in your reference.
- **Transcript:** timestamped lines with the current one in amber, plus a search box at the bottom, like the reference's message box.
- **Player controls:** the same buttons as the watch page (Stop captions, captions, transcript, fullscreen).

They come in one at a time when the page loads: the stage comes into focus, then the panel, video, controls, popup and transcript. With reduced motion turned on, everything shows without animating.

**Responsive**

| Width | Layout |
|---|---|
| 1280px and up | The full split layout, like your reference |
| 1024 to 1279px | Panel content on top. Below it, video and controls on the left, and popup and transcript in a column on the right, like the real watch page |
| Tablet | The popup and transcript sit side by side under the video |
| Phone | Everything stacks, and the popup overlaps the bottom of the video a little |

I checked phone, tablet, 1024, 1280 and 1440 widths. Nothing runs off the side, there are no console errors, and it typechecks.

**Also changed**
- The fix for the double outline on the focused link box is still in place.
- The privacy section now has an anchor so the new "Privacy" link scrolls to it.

The work is in [page.tsx](src/app/page.tsx) (`HeroProduct`, `VideoFrame`, `ExtensionPopup`, `TranscriptCard`, `PlayerControls`) and the backdrop styles in [globals.css](src/app/globals.css).

content.text:
The home page now fills exactly one screen, the nav links swap the left panel like tabs, and the demo on the right works. Nothing is committed yet.

**Full screen and tabs**
- On wide screens (1280px and up) the stage fills the whole browser window with no scrolling. The sections and footer that used to sit below the hero are gone.
- "How it works", "Privacy" and the "Get the Chrome extension" button now replace the panel's content instead of scrolling down to it. The Earshot logo takes you back to the start. The active tab gets an amber underline.
- Each tab has its own web address (`/#how`, `/#privacy`, `/#extension`), so you can link straight to one.
- On phones and tablets the panel sits on top with the demo below it, and the tabs still swap the panel.
- The footer line ("Earshot is open source…") moved into the Privacy tab.
- On very wide screens like your 2000px one, the headline and the demo cards get a bit bigger so the stage doesn't look empty.

**Interactive demo**
I split the demo into separate pieces that share one pretend video. Three subagents each made one part clickable while I built the tabs, and I tested the result in the browser.
- **Video:** captions write in word by word in time with the video. Click the video to pause or play it. Click or drag the progress bar to jump around; arrow keys work too.
- **Extension popup:** the on/off switch works. Turning it off stops the captions on the video, changes the badge to "Off", and shows the real popup's "Turn on to caption…" message.
- **Transcript:** new lines appear as they're spoken. Clicking a line jumps the video there. Search highlights matching words, and Download saves a .txt file.
- **Controls:** Stop/Start captions stays in sync with the popup switch. CC hides the captions, the transcript button hides the transcript card, and full screen enlarges the whole demo.
- When captions are off, the sound meter stops moving.
- The talk in the demo is made up, so it doesn't quote the real TED talk.

**Two notes**
- I left the hydration warning alone, as you asked. It appears because your ColorZilla extension adds an attribute to the page.
- I checked phone, 1024, 1280, 1440 and 1920 widths. Nothing runs off the side and it typechecks. I didn't try the full screen button, because the test browser can't enter full screen without a real click.

The new files are [HeroPanel.tsx](apps/web/src/components/HeroPanel.tsx) and everything in [hero-demo/](apps/web/src/components/hero-demo/). [page.tsx](apps/web/src/app/page.tsx) now just puts the two together.
